terms.d: A tiny language model I built from scratch — written and trained on the IWB Dictionary and Signature spec text. An independent model, not affiliated with Meta.
A neural network trained on huge amounts of text so it can generate human-like writing, answer questions, and follow instructions.
The neural network design behind modern language models, built from stacked blocks that weigh how every word relates to every other word.
The mechanism that lets a model decide which words in a sentence matter most when understanding or generating the next word.
Attention applied within a single sequence, so each word can look at the other words around it for context.
Running several attention operations in parallel so the model can track different kinds of word relationships at once.
In attention, the vector representing the word currently asking: which other words should I pay attention to.
In attention, the vector each word offers up so the querying word can judge how relevant it is.
In attention, the actual information a word contributes once it has been judged relevant by the query.
A list of numbers that captures a word's meaning, learned so that similar words end up with similar numbers.
The embedding looked up for each input token before the model starts processing the sequence.
Extra information added to embeddings so the model knows the order of words, since attention itself has no sense of position.
A way of encoding word position by rotating the query and key vectors, which handles long sequences gracefully.
A learned or fixed vector added per position, giving each slot in the sequence its own identity.
A step that rescales a layer's outputs to a steady range, keeping training stable and fast.
A lighter cousin of layer normalization that rescales by the root-mean-square, skipping the mean subtraction.
The per-position mini-network inside each transformer block that transforms the attention output into richer features.
A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, letting gradients flow cleanly through very deep networks.
The transformer half that generates output one token at a time, each step looking back at what it already wrote.
The transformer half that reads a whole input at once, building a rich understanding before anything is generated.
A language model built from decoders alone, which predicts the next token — the design behind Signature Llama and most chat models.
A model with both halves: the encoder reads the input, the decoder writes the output, as in translation systems.
A rule during training that hides future tokens, so the model can only learn from the past — the way real generation works.
The math that turns raw model scores into probabilities that sum to one, used to pick the next token.
The raw, unnormalized scores the model produces for every vocabulary word before softmax turns them into probabilities.
The internal vector a layer produces for each position — the model's working understanding as text flows through.
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering both the prompt and what it has generated.
A single learned number inside the model; Signature Llama v1 has about three million of them.
A parameter that scales a connection between neurons, learned during training.
A learned offset added after a weighted sum, giving each neuron its own starting push.
A bend applied to a neuron's output, like ReLU or GELU, that lets the network learn non-straight-line patterns.
An activation that passes positive numbers through unchanged and turns negatives to zero — simple and fast.
A smooth, curved activation popular in transformers that weights inputs by how likely they are under a bell curve.
An activation that multiplies the input by its own sigmoid, giving a smooth gate that many modern models prefer.
A gated feed-forward variant that splits the signal into two paths and multiplies them, boosting model quality.
A training trick that randomly switches off some neurons, forcing the network to not lean on any single one.
One of the parallel attention units inside a layer, each free to specialize in a different relationship between words.
Stored keys and values from tokens already processed, so generation does not recompute them at every step.
An attention style where several query heads share one key-value head, shrinking the cache with little quality loss.
The extreme version: every query head shares a single key-value head for maximum generation speed.
Attention limited to a recent window of tokens, letting the model handle very long texts cheaply.
Attention that deliberately skips most token pairs, computing only the connections that matter.
Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another, linking e.g. a question to a document.
A design with many small specialist networks where only a few activate per token, growing capacity without growing cost per token.
One specialist feed-forward network inside a mixture-of-experts layer, typically good at certain topics or patterns.
The tiny network in a mixture-of-experts model that picks which experts handle each token.
Placing normalization before the attention and feed-forward steps inside each block — the modern stable choice.
The older layout that normalizes after each block's residual addition.
One repeating unit of the model: attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped with normalization and residuals.
The final layer that converts the last hidden state into a score for every word in the vocabulary.
The big lookup table mapping every token ID to its learned embedding vector.
Reusing the same matrix for input embeddings and the output projection, saving parameters.
A position method that biases attention scores by distance instead of adding position vectors, extrapolating to longer texts.
A technique that stretches a trained model's context window by rescaling its rotary position embeddings.
The process of feeding a model huge amounts of text and adjusting its parameters until it predicts language well.
The first, longest training phase, where a model learns general language by predicting the next token across a giant corpus.
Extra training on a smaller, focused dataset to teach a pretrained model a particular skill, tone, or task.
Fine-tuning on examples of instructions paired with good responses, so the model learns to follow directions helpfully.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer the answers humans rate highest.
Direct preference optimization — a simpler way to teach human preferences that skips the separate reward model RLHF needs.
The score the training process tries to minimize, measuring how wrong the model's predictions are.
The standard loss for language models: it punishes the model according to how unlikely it thought the true next token was.
The core learning algorithm: nudge every parameter a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeat billions of times.
The technique that figures out how much each parameter contributed to an error, so gradient descent knows what to adjust.
How big each parameter update is — too large and training blows up, too small and it crawls.
A plan that changes the learning rate over time, usually warming up first and cooling down toward the end.
Starting training with a tiny learning rate that ramps up, which keeps the early steps stable.
A popular optimizer that adapts the learning rate per parameter using running averages of recent gradients.
Adam with weight decay handled properly — the default optimizer for training most transformers.
One full pass through the entire training dataset.
A group of examples processed together in one training step, balancing speed against memory.
A small batch used in practice, since whole-dataset batches would never fit in memory.
Adding up gradients over several small batches before updating, faking a big batch on limited hardware.
Training with a blend of 16-bit and 32-bit numbers to go faster and use less memory without hurting quality.
16-bit floating point numbers — half the memory of FP32, standard for fast training.
Brain float 16: a 16-bit format with the wide range of 32-bit, safer than FP16 for training.
A saved snapshot of the model's parameters during training, so work is never lost and the best version can be kept.
When a model memorizes its training data instead of learning general patterns, doing worse on anything new.
When a model is too small or undertrained to capture the patterns in its data.
Any technique, like dropout or weight decay, that discourages overfitting and keeps the model general.
A gentle penalty on large parameters during training that keeps the model simpler and more general.
Capping the size of gradient updates so one wild batch cannot wreck the model.
Splitting batches across many GPUs that each hold a full copy of the model and sync their updates.
Splitting the model itself across GPUs when it is too big for one card.
Assigning different layers to different GPUs, with activations flowing through like an assembly line.
Fully sharded data parallel: spreading the model's parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs to train giants.
Low-rank adaptation — fine-tuning by training tiny add-on matrices instead of the whole model, cheap and effective.
LoRA on a quantized model, letting a big model be fine-tuned on a single modest GPU.
A small trainable module inserted into a frozen model, so new skills can be added without retraining everything.
Fine-tuning on labeled examples of inputs and ideal outputs — the straightforward way to teach a task.
More pretraining on new data after the first round, e.g. to teach a model a specialty like medicine or law.
Feeding training data in order from easy to hard, the way a student learns.
The total number of tokens a training run will process — the main dial controlling cost and quality.
The full collection of text a model learns from; Signature Llama's is the IWB Dictionary plus the Signature spec archive.
Data kept out of training and used to check whether the model is genuinely learning or just memorizing.
The loss measured on the validation set — the honest scoreboard during training.
Halting training when validation stops improving, keeping the best checkpoint instead of overfitting further.
Gradually lowering the learning rate late in training so the model settles into its best settings.
A learning-rate plan that follows a cosine curve: warm up, cruise, then glide smoothly down to near zero.
The algorithm that turns gradients into parameter updates — AdamW being the usual choice.
An optimizer trick that keeps updates moving in a consistent direction, smoothing out noisy gradients.
The per-parameter measure of which way the loss would drop fastest — the compass for every update.
Running input through the model to produce predictions, the first half of every training step.
Propagating the error back through the model to compute gradients, the second half of every training step.
Feeding the model the true previous tokens during training instead of its own guesses, which stabilizes learning.
The fundamental training task: given all tokens so far, predict the next one — the skill behind everything language models do.
Running a trained model to generate answers — the doing phase, as opposed to the learning phase of training.
The model's act of producing text token by token during inference.
Choosing the next token from the model's probability distribution, with settings like temperature shaping the choice.
A dial on randomness: low values make the model pick the most likely token, high values make it more creative and surprising.
Only letting the model choose among the k most likely next tokens, cutting off the weird tail of the distribution.
Nucleus sampling: choosing from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, adapting to the model's confidence.
Always picking the single most likely next token — fast and deterministic, but sometimes dull or repetitive.
Keeping several candidate sequences alive and expanding the best ones, trading speed for higher-quality output.
Sending each generated token to the user the moment it is produced, instead of waiting for the whole answer.
How long you wait for an answer — the delay between asking and getting the first token back.
How many tokens the system can generate per second across all users.
The plain speedometer of generation: how many tokens the model produces each second.
How quickly the first token appears after a request — what makes a chat feel snappy or sluggish.
The input text you give the model, which it continues or responds to.
Hidden instructions set by the developer that shape the model's role and behavior for the whole conversation.
The text the model generates in response to a prompt.
A string that tells generation to halt the moment it appears, like a period at the end of one answer.
A cap on how many tokens the model may generate in one response.
A setting that lowers the score of tokens already used, discouraging the model from repeating itself.
A penalty applied once to any token that has appeared, pushing the model toward fresh topics.
A penalty that grows the more a token repeats, taming loops without banning words outright.
The starting number for the random generator — same seed plus same settings gives the same answer.
Generation settings, like temperature zero, that produce the same output every time for the same input.
Generation that rolls the dice each token, so the same prompt can give different answers.
A speedup trick where a small model drafts tokens and the big model just verifies them.
Processing many requests together in one go to use the hardware efficiently.
A server trick that slots new requests into the batch the moment old ones finish, keeping the GPU always busy.
Reusing the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix instead of recomputing it every time.
Shrinking a model's numbers to fewer bits, e.g. 8 or 4, so it runs faster and fits in less memory.
Storing weights as 8-bit integers — about a quarter the size of 32-bit floats, the format Signature Llama ships in.
Squeezing weights to 4 bits for the smallest, fastest models, with a small quality tradeoff.
A popular file format for quantized models that runs efficiently on ordinary computers.
An open format for exchanging trained models between different frameworks and runtimes.
The software that loads a model and generates text with it — sigllama.js is Signature Llama's engine.
The environment executing the model, whether a browser, a phone, or a server.
How many tokens of conversation the model can actually keep in mind at generation time.
Packing background documents into the prompt so the model answers from provided material.
The craft of wording inputs to get better outputs from a model.
Showing the model a few examples inside the prompt so it copies the pattern.
Asking the model to do something with no examples, relying on what it learned in training.
Asking the model to reason step by step out loud, which improves hard problems.
Telling the model who to be, like a tutor or a pirate, to shape its voice and behavior.
Manually boosting or suppressing specific tokens' scores to steer generation.
Forcing the model to answer in a strict format like JSON so programs can use the result directly.
A generation setting that guarantees the output is valid JSON.
Letting the model request real actions, like checking weather, by emitting structured calls a program executes.
The broader ability of a model to operate external tools — search, calculators, code runners — during a conversation.
When a model states something false with total confidence, inventing facts that were never in its training.
Tying a model's answers to real sources or data so it invents less.
The special end-of-sequence token whose appearance tells generation to stop.
The special beginning-of-sequence token marking where a text starts.
Seeing each token type out live as the model generates it, the effect behind the onToken callback.
The basic unit a language model reads and writes — a word, word piece, or single character depending on the tokenizer.
The tool that chops raw text into tokens before the model sees it, and turns tokens back into text afterward.
The act of splitting text into tokens — the first step of everything a language model does.
The full set of tokens a model knows, each with its own ID and learned embedding.
A token smaller than a word, like un plus believable, which lets models handle rare words by assembling pieces.
A tokenizer algorithm that starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most common pair, building the vocabulary bottom-up.
A subword tokenizer that merges the pair which most improves the training likelihood, used by BERT-style models.
A tokenizer library that treats the raw text as-is, spaces included, and learns subwords without pre-splitting words.
Tokenizing text one character at a time — simple, tiny vocabulary, and the approach Signature Llama v1 uses.
Tokenizing whole words at once, which needs a huge vocabulary and chokes on words it never saw.
The number standing in for a token inside the model — text becomes lists of IDs before any math happens.
Converting the model's output token IDs back into readable text.
A large collection of text assembled for training or study — the model's reading material.
An organized collection of examples used to train or test a model.
The actual text the model learns from during training.
Removing junk, duplicates, and garbage from training text so the model learns from quality material.
Deleting repeated passages from training data, since heavy repetition teaches the model to parrot.
The recipe of how much web text, books, code, and other sources go into the training corpus.
Training text generated by another AI rather than written by humans — useful, but risky if overused.
When test questions leak into training data, making benchmark scores look better than they really are.
One coherent piece of text in the corpus, like an article or a dictionary entry.
A fixed-size slice of text cut from documents to feed the model during training.
An ordered list of token IDs — the actual input format the model consumes.
How many tokens long a training sequence is; longer sequences teach longer-range patterns.
Filler tokens added to make all sequences in a batch the same length.
Cutting a sequence down to the maximum length the model accepts.
Gluing several short documents into one training sequence so no space goes to waste.
A marker telling the model which positions are real text and which are just padding to ignore.
A reserved token with a job, like marking the start or end of a sequence.
The fallback token for text the tokenizer cannot represent — rare in subword and character schemes.
The special token used to fill sequences out to equal length in a batch.
A token marking boundaries between segments, like the question and the passage.
A special token whose final state is used as the summary of a whole input for classification.
Representing unknown characters as raw bytes so the tokenizer never truly fails on odd text.
How many tokens a tokenizer produces per word on average — lower means cheaper, faster processing.
How compactly a tokenizer encodes text, measured in characters per token.
How the tokenizer treats spaces and line breaks — getting it wrong garbles code and poetry.
Standardizing text before tokenizing, like unifying quotes or unicode forms.
Whether the tokenizer distinguishes Apple from apple — a choice that changes the vocabulary.
The universal character standard that lets tokenizers handle every language's script.
How many distinct tokens the model knows — bigger vocabularies read efficiently but need bigger embedding tables.
Words the tokenizer never learned, which older word-level systems could not represent at all.
A run of n consecutive tokens or words, the classic unit of old-school language statistics.
The code that streams training examples from disk into the GPU fast enough to keep it busy.
Randomizing the order of training examples so the model does not learn spurious patterns from the ordering.
One complete pass over the training data, after which shuffling usually starts a fresh order.
Examples reserved from training so they can honestly test what the model learned.
The correct answer attached to a training example, like the true next token.
The token IDs fed into the model for one training or inference step.
The token IDs the model is supposed to predict — the answers for its input IDs.
Standardized test sets the whole field uses to compare models fairly.
Measuring how good a model actually is, with tests rather than vibes.
A standard test suite the whole field runs so models can be compared on equal footing.
How surprised a model is by real text, on average — lower means it predicts language better.
The fraction of test questions the model gets right — the simplest score there is.
A strict score that only counts answers identical to the expected one.
A balance of precision and recall into one number, common for question-answering tests.
A classic translation score based on how many word sequences the output shares with reference translations.
A summarization score measuring overlap between the model's summary and human-written ones.
A famous 57-subject multiple-choice test of general knowledge, from math to law to history.
A commonsense test asking the model to pick the most sensible ending to everyday situations.
Grade-school science questions, in easy and challenge flavors, testing reasoning over memorization.
A test of whether the model repeats common myths or tells the truth about tricky questions.
A coding benchmark where the model must write programs that pass hidden tests.
Grade-school math word problems testing whether the model can reason step by step.
The locked-away questions used for final scoring, never seen during training.
Testing the model with no examples in the prompt, pure cold.
Testing with a few examples in the prompt, the standard fair-comparison setup.
Having real people rate model answers — slow and pricey, but the gold standard for quality.
Using a strong model to grade other models' answers, a fast stand-in for human raters.
A chess-style skill score from head-to-head model comparisons, as used on public leaderboards.
How often one model's answer is preferred over another's in side-by-side tests.
The chance that at least one of k generated attempts solves the problem — the coding benchmark staple.
Whether the model's confidence matches its actual accuracy — a well-calibrated model knows when it is guessing.
How well the model holds up on odd, adversarial, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Ways a test can mislead — leaked data, judge favoritism, or questions that reward the wrong thing.
Measuring how often a model produces hateful, abusive, or otherwise harmful text.
Deliberately attacking a model with tricky prompts to find its failure and safety holes before the public does.
A prompt crafted to slip past a model's safety training and make it do what it was told not to.
Hiding malicious instructions inside data the model reads, tricking it into obeying the attacker.
Testing that a model refuses genuinely dangerous requests while staying useful.
How well the model's goals line up with what humans actually want — helpful, honest, and safe.
Whether the model actually moves the user toward their goal, not just whether it sounds fluent.
The property of not causing damage — refusing real harm while staying useful for everything else.
The model saying what it believes is true and admitting uncertainty instead of bluffing.
When safety tuning goes too far and the model refuses perfectly innocent requests.
The model's bad habit of agreeing with the user even when the user is wrong.
A simple reference model or score that a new approach must beat to prove it is worth anything.
Removing one piece of a system at a time to measure what each piece actually contributes.
The observed rule that bigger models, more data, and more compute predictably lower the loss.
The finding that models should be trained on far more tokens than was fashionable — about twenty tokens per parameter.
The sweet spot of model size versus training data for a fixed compute budget.
A skill that appears suddenly once a model gets big enough, absent in smaller versions.
The software framework that runs benchmarks consistently so scores are comparable.
The log-probability the model assigned to a token — the raw material of many evaluations.
Testing by asking the model to pick from options, scored by which choice gets the highest probability.
Testing by letting the model write freely and judging the result, closer to real use.
Verifying the test questions were not hiding in the training data.
Re-running old evaluations after each change to make sure nothing that worked got broken.
Showing users two versions and measuring which performs better in the real world.
Which answer real people pick — the signal behind RLHF and preference training.
A small, carefully human-verified set of examples treated as ground truth for testing.
Putting a trained model where real users can reach it — the trip from lab to the world.
Running a model behind an endpoint that answers requests, day and night.
A programming interface letting other software send prompts and receive completions.
The secret token identifying who is calling an API — Signature Llama needs none, since it runs locally.
The web address a model listens on for incoming requests.
Software built to load models and serve many users efficiently, with batching and caching.
A fast open-source serving engine famous for its paged attention memory management.
A lean C++ engine that runs quantized models on ordinary CPUs — the offline-everywhere workhorse.
A friendly tool that downloads and runs open models locally with one command.
The big public hub where the AI world shares models, datasets, and demos.
Any repository where trained models are published for others to download and use.
Releasing the trained parameters so anyone can download, study, and run the model themselves.
A model whose code and often weights are public — Signature Llama's engine and trainer are published this way.
The legal terms saying what you may do with a model — commercial use, modification, and redistribution rules.
Using a model to make money, which some licenses allow freely and others restrict.
Running the model on the device at the network's edge — phones, laptops, gadgets — instead of a data center.
The model running entirely on the user's own hardware, private and offline-capable.
Running the model inside a web page with JavaScript — Signature Llama's home turf, no install needed.
The browser API that unlocks the graphics card for fast in-page computation.
A compact binary format letting near-native-speed code, like inference kernels, run in the browser.
Shrinking and tuning a model so it runs well on phones with limited memory and battery.
The deployment-time step of converting weights to fewer bits for speed and size.
Deleting the least important weights or neurons to slim a model down.
Training a small student model to imitate a big teacher, keeping most of the quality at a fraction of the size.
The formal name for the teacher-student transfer technique behind many compact models.
Blending the weights of two trained models to combine their skills without retraining.
Packaging a model and its environment into a portable container that runs the same anywhere.
The standard container tool for shipping software, models included, with identical environments.
The graphics processor — the parallel-compute workhorse that trains and serves nearly all big models.
A GPU's own memory, where the model and its working data must fit during training and serving.
Running the model on the regular processor — slower than GPU but available everywhere.
A neural processing unit: a chip built specifically to accelerate AI math on devices.
Google's tensor processing unit, a custom chip designed for massive-scale training.
What you pay per request or per token to run a model — zero for a model running in your own browser.
The unit price of generation on hosted APIs, usually quoted per million tokens.
How many requests an API allows per minute — a non-issue when the model lives on your device.
The fraction of time a serving endpoint is actually reachable.
Watching a deployed model for errors, slowness, and quality drift.
Recording requests and outputs so problems can be diagnosed and behavior audited.
Labeling each trained model, like v1 and v2, so you can track and roll between them.
Switching back to the previous model version when a new one misbehaves.
Sending a new model to a small slice of users first to catch problems early.
Adding more serving capacity as demand grows.
Automatically spinning servers up and down with demand.
The traffic cop spreading requests across many model servers.
The slow first request while a model loads into memory.
Fast requests once the model is already loaded and ready.
Storing answers to repeated questions so identical prompts return instantly.
A content delivery network that serves static files, like model weights, from servers near each user.
The model working with no internet at all — possible once the files are downloaded.
A progressive web app: a website that installs and behaves like a native app, offline included.
Serving a site as plain files with no server code — how every Signature site, including this one, is published.
